extracted.intended_audience: information scientists, librarians, historians of stenography, professional stenographers and indexing/abstracting practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and comparing shorthand/stenography systems (and related notational shorthands) by their design goals, usability, domain fit, and technological adaptability, using historical and practical examples from diverse systems (Pitman, Gregg, WLN, SSS, steno machines, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aims of shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorthand aims to reduce redundancy in ordinary writing and 'to convey as much information as possible with the smallest amount of writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay frames these as the two major aims; evaluate a system by how well it compresses verbal/written content while retaining meaning. Examples: systems that omit vowels or use diacriticals to shorten words. Anti-pattern: systems that are concise but lose essential information or become indecipherable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of learning / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: How easy the system is for people who are not extensively educated to learn and use; some systems require extensive study while others claim rapid mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claims and real-world training time (e.g., Notescript claims mastery in 12 hours; classic Gregg and Pitman required substantial study). Consider target learners (office clerks vs professional reporters). Anti-pattern: highly prescriptive systems that deter wide adoption due to learning difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and suitability for real-time reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The system's ability to keep up with spoken language in environments such as court reporting, parliamentary proceedings, or journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate on achievable writing/recording speed and practical use-cases: manual shorthand vs stenotype machines (stenotype and stenotypy permit much higher throughput). Example: steno machines and stenotypy allowed faster proceedings recording. Systems intended for court reporting must support very high transcription rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim fidelity and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of the system to capture verbatim speech or detailed content accurately without introducing distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether system design (e.g., omission of vowels, heavy abbreviation) compromises verbatim capture. Historical anti-pattern: inadequate transcriptions leading to corrupted texts (possible factor in 'bad' quartos of Shakespeare). Positive examples: trained parliamentary reporters producing faithful records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose/genre fit (specialization vs general-purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the system is optimized for specific tasks (court reporting, business dictation, note-taking, scientific notation) or general-purpose use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match system features to intended use: Gregg favored for office/clerical use, Pitman associated with court/reporting, WLN for chemical structure indexing, SSS for physiology/medicine. A good fit increases efficiency; poor fit forces workarounds or errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness versus decipherability trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance between maximum compactness (omitting vowels, using arbitraries) and the ease of later deciphering/decoding notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how much contextual memory or specialist knowledge is required to interpret notes. Systems that heavily omit vowels or use many arbitraries may be compact but place burden on memory/context—risking later unreadability. Guidance: prefer designs that balance compression with reliable decode cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific expressiveness (notation for science/medicine/math)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to represent specialized content (chemical structures, mathematical notation, physiological conditions, laboratory procedures) clearly and succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Wiswesser Line Notation (WLN) provides compact, unambiguous chemical-structure notation suitable for indexing and retrieval; Symbolic Shorthand System (SSS) provides mnemonic signs for physiology (e.g., 'Cr' for cardiac). Evaluate whether a shorthand supports needed domain concepts and operations (substructure search, procedural depiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity and suitability for indexing/computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the notation maps unambiguously to the represented concept and can be used by machines (indexing, retrieval) or typed on keyboards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WLN is cited as a compact, unambiguous representation aligned to typewriter keys and useful for online indexing/retrieval; evaluate systems for machine-readability, unique mapping, and conversion to structural diagrams (e.g., DARC/WLN conversion programs). Anti-pattern: ambiguous or highly context-dependent notations that hinder automated processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability to technology and survivability
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the shorthand system adapts to new technologies (tape recorders, dictation machines, stenotype, voice recognition, computerization) and survives technological change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a system integrates with machines (stenotype compatibility), or whether its role is diminished by recording/voice tech. Consider historical persistence (systems that adapted—WLN & stenotype use—survived). Predictive guidance: systems that cannot adapt to digital/voice workflows risk obsolescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachability and institutional support
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of teaching infrastructure, official adoption (schools, legal/court appointments), and societal support that enable widespread learning and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: growth through high-school classes, laws appointing official court reporters, organizations promoting systems (Pitman, Gregg). Evaluate availability of courses, certification, institutional appointments which amplify adoption. Anti-pattern: lack of institutional backing limiting spread despite technical merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation ergonomics and practical workplace constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical considerations such as whether the method is disquieting in client-facing settings, physical ergonomics, and equipment constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: suggestion that using a steno machine in a client-present meeting might be disconcerting; lab safety/context may preclude certain devices. Evaluate whether a system or device is suitable given professional interactions, privacy, or safety concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization, officialization and establishment of reporting roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a system is standardized, has official roles (e.g., official shorthand reporters for courts/parliament) and published organized materials (journals, periodicals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence: Gurney firm's official appointment to Old Bailey and Houses of Parliament aided spread; periodicals and promotional campaigns (Pitman vs Gregg) influenced market share. Evaluate presence of standards, official appointments, and professional networks that help adoption and quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociocultural acceptance and perceived prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: How social attitudes (gender norms, machismo, prestige of shorthand as route to success) influence who learns shorthand and how widely it is adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes shorthand was a 'route to success' and that cultural shifts (machismo, automation) changed perceptions. Evaluate likelihood of adoption given contemporary social perceptions and perceived career benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness for domain-specific procedures/graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to encode procedures, apparatus, and graphical operations compactly (laboratory procedures, beakers, crystallize, condensers) in a shorthand form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Baltazzi's chemical shorthand uses graphical signs for apparatus/procedures; evaluate whether such symbolic systems can capture procedural sequences succinctly and unambiguously. Consider readability and whether symbols overlap or cause confusion.
